document.title: Afghanistan: Observers Report Uptick in Support for Anti-Taliban Factions by Iran
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
document.note: [Confidential] Relays information about Iranian military and political support for anti-Taliban factions. A State source sees it as a strategic reaction to Taliban efforts to control the north, while Pakistanis see it as aggressive.

persons.name: Abdul Rashid Dostam
persons.role: Former leader of the National Islamic Movement of Afghanistan (NIMA/Junbish), ousted in late May 1997
persons.status_detail: Described as ousted in late May 1997

mentions.quote: SINCE THE OUSTER OF GENERAL DOSTAM, THE FORMER NATIONAL ISLAMIC MOVEMENT OF AFGHANISTAN (NIMA) LEADER, IN LATE MAY.

persons.role: Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister; point man for Iranian efforts to unite anti-Taliban factions into a new 'government'

events.description: Taliban entered Mazar-i-Sharif in late May and were subsequently pushed back; General Dostam ousted as NIMA leader.
Iran closed its border with Afghanistan to all traffic in early June.
A July 4 conversation between the Embassy and an observer in which the observer reiterated that Iran will not allow its allies to be defeated without a fight.
US Embassy Islamabad cable reports an uptick in Iranian military and political support for anti-Taliban factions.
Observer visited Bamiyan in mid-June and heard of many Iranians living in the town.
Iran closed its border with Afghanistan to all traffic; reportedly still closed.
Iran established a forward base in Meshed for all ministries working on Afghan issues.
US Embassy Islamabad cable reporting observers' views on Iranian policy-making on Afghanistan.
Dostam ousted as NIMA leader; Taliban entered Mazar-i-Sharif in late May and were subsequently defeated and pushed back.
Iranian flights between Iran and Afghan points increased, reportedly carrying small arms, ammunition and explosives; Iranian military aircraft seen at Mazar-i-Sharif and Bamiyan airports.
Deputy FM Borujerdi visited Mazar-i-Sharif and Bamiyan several times in the six weeks before the cable to push a new anti-Taliban government.
Velayati met anti-Taliban leaders including Hekmatyar and Rabbani.
Conversation with an observer on Iranian involvement and Pakistan's support for the Taliban.
US Embassy Islamabad cable reporting uptick in Iranian support for anti-Taliban factions.

sources_cited: Unnamed observers of the Afghan scene in conversations with US Embassy Islamabad political officer
key_claims: Observers report increased Iranian military and political support to anti-Taliban factions since the ouster of Dostam and the Taliban's defeat at Mazar-i-Sharif in late May 1997.
Iranian flights, including reported military aircraft at Mazar-i-Sharif and Bamiyan, are believed to carry small arms, ammunition and explosives alongside humanitarian items.
Iran has reportedly increased staff at its Mazar-i-Sharif and Bamiyan consulates, with some suspected links to the Revolutionary Guards.
Iran is pushing the factions to form a rival government to the Taliban, led diplomatically by Deputy FM Borujerdi, while FM Velayati meets Hekmatyar and Rabbani.
Observers split on whether Iranian involvement is defensive (protecting allies) or aggressive (seeking dominance in northern Afghanistan and a land bridge to Tajikistan).
Iranian anti-Americanism, including belief that the US backs the Taliban to enable UNOCAL pipelines, is a motivating factor.
Iranian Afghan policy is driven by security agencies, the Revolutionary Guards and the Interior Ministry rather than the Foreign Ministry or President Khatami, with a forward base in Meshed.
